Practices.Summary: Glean uses a structured pull-request review workflow for public repositories. Contributors must fork the repo, create a feature or bugfix branch (e.g., `git checkout -b feature/my-feature`), commit following TypeScript style rules, and open a PR against the main branch. Every PR must be reviewed by at least one member of the `@gleanwork/gleanwork-reviewers` team before merging, as enforced by a CODEOWNERS rule (`* @gleanwork/gleanwork-reviewers`) covering all files. The PR template requires authors to fill in: Description, Related Issue (closes #), Motivation and Context, Type of Change (bug fix / new feature / breaking change / documentation / refactoring / CI / build), How Has This Been Tested (unit / integration / manual), a Checklist (code style, docs updated, tests added, breaking-change notes), Screenshots, and Additional Notes.

evidence.quote: * @gleanwork/gleanwork-reviewers
git checkout -b feature/my-feature

- [ ] My code follows the code style of this project
- [ ] I have updated the documentation accordingly
- [ ] I have added tests to cover my changes

Practices.Summary: Glean ships a Pull Request Review agent and a Resolve GitHub PR Feedback agent that the team itself uses to keep review quality consistent as the org scales. The PR review agent scans code changes, suggests improvements, and flags risk areas. The resolve-feedback agent aggregates unresolved comments, classifies them by priority, and generates an actionable checklist with file references so engineers can close out reviews faster.

evidence.quote: Pull request reviews remain one of the most common sources of delay. Reviewers need to understand code changes in context, assess alignment with design intent, and ensure consistency with existing standards.
The pull request review agent scans code changes, suggests improvements, and flags areas that may need closer attention to support faster, more consistent reviews.

The resolve GitHub PR feedback agent aggregates unresolved comments, classifies them by priority, and generates an actionable checklist with file references and relevant context so engineers can close out reviews faster.

Tools.Summary: GitHub is the primary code-review platform. ESLint and Prettier are the enforced linters/formatters for TypeScript code: linting runs as the first step of CI on every PR (Node 20/22/24 matrix via `ci.yml`), and Prettier auto-formats on every merge to main via the `format-on-merge.yml` workflow. JSDoc is required for all public API surfaces. Glean's own Pull Request Review and Resolve GitHub PR Feedback agents augment the human review workflow.

evidence.quote: We use ESLint and Prettier for code formatting and linting.
Add JSDoc comments to public API methods and classes.
Glean accelerates software engineering workflows with context-aware agents that work across the systems engineers already use — repositories, tickets, documents, and communication tools.

Stakeholders.Summary: All code changes must be reviewed by `@gleanwork/gleanwork-reviewers` (the Glean internal team that owns all files in the repo). External contributors and open-source users submit PRs from forks; the Glean maintainer team reviews and merges. For distributed engineering teams, the AI PR review and PR-feedback agents help reviewers maintain consistency as teams scale.

evidence.quote: * @gleanwork/gleanwork-reviewers
As teams scale, review quality becomes uneven and feedback cycles lengthen.

Others.Summary: The PR template's Type of Change section classifies every contribution into one of seven categories: 'Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)', 'New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)', 'Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to change)', 'Documentation update', 'Refactoring (no functional changes)', 'CI/CD changes', and 'Build system changes'. This taxonomy aligns change classification with downstream communication such as release notes and breaking-change warnings. Additionally, Dependabot automates dependency updates on a monthly npm schedule with cooldown periods (patch: 3 days, minor: 7 days, major: 30 days) and groups dev-dependency updates to reduce review noise.

Issues.Issue_Title: Global token auth sends wrong header: X-Glean-Act-As instead of X-Glean-ActAs
Issues.Description: When using global-token authentication, the MCP server was sending the header `X-Glean-Act-As` (hyphenated) instead of the correct `X-Glean-ActAs` (camelCased), causing 400 Bad Request errors for all impersonated API calls. The root cause was first reported in issue #263 and fixed in PR #264, available from v0.8.0 onwards.

Issues.Issue_Title: npm install fails: Unsupported workspace:* dependency in @gleanwork/local-mcp-server@0.9.0
Issues.Description: The published npm package `@gleanwork/local-mcp-server@0.9.0` contained a `workspace:*` pnpm monorepo protocol dependency that leaked into the published artifact. npm cannot resolve this protocol, causing `npm install` to fail with EUNSUPPORTEDPROTOCOL. The bug was fixed the same day and released as v0.9.1.

Issues.Issue_Title: [BUG] GLEAN_ACT_AS header seems to be incorrect
Issues.Description: Root-cause issue for #347. The `X-Glean-ActAs` HTTP header name was implemented as `X-Glean-Act-As` throughout the global-token authentication path, causing all act-as impersonation calls to return 400 errors. Fixed in PR #264 (merged Aug 26, 2025).

AgentSeal adversarial scan flagged that `people_profile_search` exposes a broad set of employee PII (email, manager_email, department) in tool outputs, raising data-minimization concerns for the local MCP server.

Issues.Issue_Title: [BUG] npx @gleanwork/local-mcp-server fails with EUNSUPPORTEDPROTOCOL for workspace:*
Issues.Description: Running `npx -y @gleanwork/local-mcp-server` fails with npm error EUNSUPPORTEDPROTOCOL: 'Unsupported URL Type "workspace:": workspace:*'. The published package leaks a pnpm workspace protocol dependency that npm cannot resolve — a recurrence of the pattern seen in issue #319.

Issues.Issue_Title: [BUG] Warnings in tests RE: requests without a request handler
Issues.Description: Test suite emits MSW warnings ('intercepted a request without a matching request handler') for unmocked OAuth authorization-server metadata requests in `src/test/auth/authorize.test.ts`, indicating incomplete request handler coverage in the test suite.

Issues.Issue_Title: Value model in AdditionalFieldDefinition is an empty class, silently drops all data
Issues.Description: The auto-generated Python SDK's `Value` model inside `AdditionalFieldDefinition` is defined as an empty class. As a result, any additional-field values passed to the API are silently dropped rather than serialized, with no error raised.

Calling `upload_files()` in the Python API client raises `httpx.RequestNotRead`, making file upload via the SDK non-functional. The issue appears to stem from how the generated client constructs the multipart request body.

Issues.Issue_Title: AnswerLikes.likedBy field validation error: Pydantic expects list but API returns null
Issues.Description: The `AnswerLikes.likedBy` field is typed as `List[str]` in the Python client's Pydantic model, but the live Glean API can return `null` for this field, causing a Pydantic `ValidationError` at runtime when deserializing API responses that include answers with no likes.

Issues.Issue_Title: [FEATURE] Adopt provider-prefixed tool names for all exposed MCP tools
Issues.Description: When integrating multiple MCP servers from different providers, generic tool names cause namespace collisions in the client's tool registry. This is a request to adopt provider-prefixed tool names across all Glean MCP tools.

Issues.Issue_Title: [FEATURE] Option to deploy MCP server as SSE
Issues.Description: In many corporate environments running local MCP servers is impractical. Request to create an SSE-based MCP server deployable via Docker to a Kubernetes cluster, with user auth handled through per-user configuration.

Follow-up to the new `configure` command (#38): support updating an existing MCP configuration when authentication credentials change, including a `--force` flag to overwrite the current configuration without manual file editing.

Practices.Summary: From the 12 analyzed issues, three recurring bug patterns emerge: (1) pnpm `workspace:*` protocol leaks into published npm packages (issues #319 and #345), causing install failures for all end-users — Glean's practice is to issue a same-day regression fix and cut a new patch release (v0.9.1 within hours of #319); (2) HTTP header name typos in the authentication layer (`X-Glean-Act-As` vs `X-Glean-ActAs`) persisted across multiple issues (#263, #347) and required explicit root-cause analysis before the final fix in PR #264; (3) auto-generated Python SDK type mismatches (null vs list, empty model classes silently dropping data) are tracked in the api-client-python repo but resolved more slowly, suggesting lower triage priority for generated code bugs. Glean engineers also associate production failures with specific release tags to isolate regression scope and ship fixes as online configuration changes for instant rollback.

evidence.quote: Errors could be associated with specific release tags, and different experiments were isolated from each other.
Rolling back a problematic release could be done instantly with an online configuration change.
Like in any implementation, there was some tuning needed to make the mechanism work well.

Tools.Summary: GitHub Issues is the primary bug tracking and triage system for public auxiliary repositories, backed by structured bug report templates (bug_report.md) that prompt reporters for: description, steps to reproduce, expected vs. actual behavior, screenshots if applicable, and environment information (OS, Node version, MCP client). Feature requests use a separate feature_request.md template. For the core Index Server, custom remapping and build tooling on top of ObjectWeb ASM handles JAR distribution via Cloud Storage, with online configuration flags enabling instant rollback without restart.

evidence.quote: We used some open source libraries (e.g. ObjectWeb ASM) to help build this remapping tool.
Enterprise memory at Glean uses reinforcement learning to find the optimal tool use strategies.
We grade the results on correctness, completeness, and efficiency, and feed the learnings back into the system in natural language—the language of LLMs.

Stakeholders.Summary: Glean's ranking, agentic engine, and platform engineering teams own bug-resolution paths for the core product, with engineering leadership publicly framing architectural tradeoffs. For public SDK and MCP repos, the `@gleanwork/gleanwork-reviewers` team triages and resolves reported issues from external contributors and enterprise customers. Community reporters (GitHub users) surface bugs via the structured issue templates, and the Glean maintainer team responds and merges fixes.

This structured intake ensures bugs contain the minimum context needed for diagnosis, reducing back-and-forth between reporters and maintainers.
